tasks.title: Observation of a star
tasks.statement: Observations were done by the naked eye on June 16, 2008, Universal time was used. An observer has registered that a star passed zenith at 0 h18m, and at 8h17m its height above the horizon was 87°12'. Find the latitude of the observations.

parts.question: Find the latitude of the observations.
parts.reference: The difference is 7859" between the two observations. It is almost exactly 1/3 of a sidereal day. During this time the star moves 120° of its daily path. And its zenith distance has changed by C = 90° - 87°12' = 2°48'. Using plane geometry, B = C / 1.732 = 1°37'. The declination of the star is equal to delta = 90° - B = 88°23'. Accordingly, this star culminates at zenith only at latitude phi = delta. However, according to the condition of our problem the observations were made with the naked eye on 16 June, when polar day appears at such northern latitudes. Therefore, correct answer is only one: -88°23' (88°23' South latitude).

tasks.title: Planetarium
tasks.statement:
Classical devices "planetaria" are arranged so that each group of stars is projected on a dome by a small optical system. Foils with hole-stars of the corresponding sizes are often used as these "slides" of constellations which are projected on the dome, so that most of the light is blocked by the foil (the black sky appears), and only light through the holes are transmitted (so stars appear). For example, images of 0m stars on the foil have the size l 0 = 0.1 mm, and stars up to 6m are demonstrated, the focal length of the projecting system is f = 25 cm, and the device has 16 separate projecting systems for every hemisphere. The dome of the planetarium of the observatory “Bobek” has a diameter of 2R = 10 m.
Let's suppose that all slides have been removed for replacement by more perfect ones, and the whole light began to be projected on the dome. What would the total stellar magnitude of the illuminated dome be (the artificial gray sky)? Would it be possible to read a newspaper in such an illuminance?
The answer has to include a list of the necessary parameters with formulae and numerical values.

parts.question: What would the total stellar magnitude of the illuminated dome be (the artificial gray sky)? Would it be possible to read a newspaper in such an illuminance?
parts.reference: Image of a star 0m in projection to the dome has diameter L = Gamma * l_0, where Gamma = R/F = 20, so L = 2 mm. The area of the illuminated surface for 0m star is S_m0 = pi L^2 / 4 = 3.14 mm^2. After slides-foils are removed, the area of the shining surface is S = 2 pi R^2 = 157 m^2. The shining area will be K = S / S_m0 = 50 000 000 times larger. In terms of stellar magnitudes: Delta m = 2.5 lg K = 19.25^m. Thus, the stellar magnitude of the dome will be 0^m - 19.25^m = -19.25^m. It gives an illuminance corresponding approximately to indoors illuminance at daytime. Of course, it is possible to read without any problem.

tasks.title: Sunrise on Mars
tasks.statement: The Polar Bear (whom was already met in the texts of many International Astronomy Olympiads) was tired to make astronomical observations on Earth. He made a fascinating journey to the North Pole of Mars, and decided to observe a sunrise there. Calculate how long this sunrise lasts. The solution has to include a picture with an image of the Bear on the North Pole of Mars. Necessary sizes or angular sizes should be in the picture. Assume that Mars is spherical and its orbit may be considered circular. Recollect for yourself the necessary information about the Polar Bear.

parts.question: Calculate how long this sunrise lasts, including a picture with an image of the Bear on the North Pole of Mars.
parts.reference: For an observer on the North Pole of Mars the angle between the ecliptic and the horizon is equal to epsilon = 25.2°. During the sunrise the Sun goes up to the angle equal to its apparent angular diameter alpha = D / L. During this time the Sun moves an angular distance phi = alpha / sin epsilon on the ecliptic. Thus, the duration of the sunrise equals to tau = phi / nu = alpha / (nu * sin epsilon), where nu is the speed of the Sun along the Martian ecliptic. Using mean values: L = 228 million km, nu = 360° / 687 days = 0.524° per day, tau = 1.57 days or 37.6 hours.

tasks.title: Photo of Jupiter
tasks.statement:
In the photo of Jupiter that was taken on October 19, 2009, one of the Galilean moons and its shadow on the disc of the planet can be seen. Jupiter was near the middle of Capricornus constellation when the photo was taken.
Find the orbital distance from the moon to the surface of the planet. Determine the name of the moon. The solution should be illustrated by drawings. The name of the moon in the solution and in the drawings should be written (or duplicated) in English.

parts.question: Find the orbital distance from the moon to the surface of the planet and determine the name of the moon.
parts.reference: Using the formulas of a rectangular triangle and the angle phi between the Sun and Jupiter (~108° based on dates/constellations), calculate the angle alpha of the Sun-Earth-Jupiter configuration. Measuring values on the photo gives a value of L/R equal to 9.64. Comparing with tables for Galilean moons: Io (5.90), Europa (9.39), Ganymede (14.97), Callisto (26.33). The proximity to 9.39 indicates the moon is Europa.

tasks.title: Jupiter disappeared
tasks.statement: Let us suppose that Jupiter suddenly disappeared. The moons of Jupiter became independent bodies.

parts.question: Which former Galileo moon(s) and in what case may leave the Solar system?
parts.reference: A body can leave the Solar system if its total energy in the field of gravitation of the Sun exceeds zero, meaning its full speed at the distance of Jupiter's orbit is at least 2^(1/2) times larger than the orbital velocity of Jupiter (18.48 km/s). For any moon such a velocity is possible in a configuration of local opposition. Answer: Io, Europa, Ganimede, Callisto, every moon in the case being in the proper sector shown at the drawing.

parts.question: Which former Galileo moon(s) and in what case may fall into the Sun?
parts.reference: A body can fall into the Sun if the velocity relative to the Sun is strongly reduced (to zero the orbital component), or if its velocity vector is directed strictly to the Sun. By the diagram of geometrical summation of velocities, falling into the Sun is possible only for Io and Europa, and for both of them it would take place only in two points (before and after local conjunctions with the Sun). Answer: Io and Europa in the case being in the points of orbit shown at the drawing.
